notice: Harm-reduction index of documented psychoactive substances, plants and fungi people encounter, common adulterants, and medicines that change interaction risk. It is not every chemical in existence, and it is not a dose, a source, or a synthesis guide. A missing interaction is unknown risk, not a clearance.

drugs.name: Morphine
drugs.summary: Morphine is filed here as a harm-reduction record. The reference opioid. Breathing slows as the effect deepens, and hospital vials and street material are not interchangeable. This is not a dose, a source, or a reason to use it.
drugs.history: Morphine is part of the public scientific and medical record, with a commonly cited date around 1804. Legal and medical status have changed over time and still differ by country. The reference opioid. Breathing slows as the effect deepens, and hospital vials and street material are not interchangeable.
drugs.legal_status: Control status depends on the country, the form, and sometimes the amount. This file is not legal advice.
drugs.medical_status: Licensed as a medicine in at least some countries. A prescription is not a clearance to mix it or to use it outside medical care.
drugs.chemistry: Opioid. Named here so the breathing risk can be recognised. Manufacture and extraction are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. The reference opioid. Breathing slows as the effect deepens, and hospital vials and street material are not interchangeable.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.history: Thebaine is part of the public scientific and medical record, with a commonly cited date around 1835. Legal and medical status have changed over time and still differ by country. An opium alkaloid used by industry as a starting material. It is toxic and convulsive, not a mild opioid. This file does not describe conversion.
drugs.legal_status: Control status depends on the country, the form, and sometimes the amount. This file is not legal advice.
drugs.medical_status: No accepted medical product. Material in circulation is unregulated and may be mislabelled or contaminated.
drugs.chemistry: Opioid. Named here so the breathing risk can be recognised. Manufacture and extraction are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. An opium alkaloid used by industry as a starting material. It is toxic and convulsive, not a mild opioid. This file does not describe conversion.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.chemistry: Benzodiazepine or closely related sedative. Named for the blackout and breathing risk. Synthesis is outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Positive modulator of GABA-A receptors. Raises the effect of the brain's main calming signal.
drugs.onset: Often within an hour for swallowed forms. Faster routes are not described here and are not safer.

effects: reduced anxiety
sleepiness
muscle relaxation
memory gaps
drugs.acute_risks: Amnesia, injury, and sexual vulnerability during blackouts. With alcohol or opioids, breathing can stop. A sleep benzodiazepine heavily restricted because of misuse and blackouts.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, worsened anxiety between uses, falls in older people, and a hard withdrawal.
drugs.overdose_signs: Extreme sedation. If an opioid or alcohol is also involved: slow breathing and unresponsiveness. That is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Dependence can develop within weeks of regular use.
drugs.tolerance: The calming effect fades. The withdrawal risk does not.
drugs.withdrawal: Rebound anxiety, insomnia, perceptual changes, and seizures. Stopping suddenly after regular use can be a medical emergency.

drugs.history: 2C-B is part of the public scientific and medical record, with a commonly cited date around 1974. Legal and medical status have changed over time and still differ by country. A psychedelic phenethylamine. Pills sold as 2C-B are often something else. Stimulation and nausea are common.
drugs.legal_status: Control status depends on the country, the form, and sometimes the amount. This file is not legal advice.
drugs.medical_status: No accepted medical product. Material in circulation is unregulated and may be mislabelled or contaminated.
drugs.chemistry: Psychedelic or psychedelic-like. Named for recognition and risk. Extraction and synthesis are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Many act as serotonin 5-HT2A agonists. Others in this list have different and sometimes more dangerous mechanisms.
drugs.onset: Minutes to more than an hour. A slow start is a common reason people take more and then have a much stronger effect.
drugs.duration: From under an hour to a full day or longer. Some, including DOB and related drugs, last much longer than LSD.
drugs.half_life: Often poorly studied outside a few medicines and classic psychedelics. Duration of impairment is the practical fact.
effects: altered perception
changed thinking
emotional intensity
sensory distortion
drugs.acute_risks: Panic, dangerous behaviour, and for some members of this class, seizures, overheating, heart strain, or vasoconstriction. NBOMe compounds and ibogaine are physically riskier than classic psychedelics. A psychedelic phenethylamine. Pills sold as 2C-B are often something else. Stimulation and nausea are common.
drugs.chronic_risks: Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder is uncommon but real. Frequent use is linked with lasting anxiety in some people.
drugs.overdose_signs: Seizures, collapse, chest pain, a limb that stays white and painful, or a temperature that keeps rising. Those are emergencies, not a 'bad trip' to wait out.
drugs.dependence: Classic psychedelics have little physical dependence. They can still be misused, and some analogues are more compulsive or more toxic.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to LSD-type psychedelics rises very fast and fades over several days. That is not a dosing instruction.
drugs.withdrawal: A physical withdrawal syndrome is not typical. Low mood and anxiety after a difficult experience are.
drugs.medical_uses: A small number are in clinical research or traditional ceremonial use. That is not a reason to use them, and it is not a dose.
drugs.contraindications: Personal or family psychosis, lithium, tramadol, MAOIs, and heart disease for the physically harsh members.
drugs.testing: Blotter and powders sold as LSD are sometimes NBOMe compounds, which are more toxic. A bitter or metallic taste is a warning, not a confirmation.
drugs.harm_reduction: A sober sitter matters. Do not mix with lithium, tramadol, or MAOIs. This file has no dose and does not describe extraction.

drugs.acute_risks: Panic, dangerous behaviour, and for some members of this class, seizures, overheating, heart strain, or vasoconstriction. drugs.chronic_risks: Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder is uncommon but real. Frequent use is linked with lasting anxiety in some people.
drugs.overdose_signs: Seizures, collapse, chest pain, a limb that stays white and painful, or a temperature that keeps rising. Those are emergencies, not a 'bad trip' to wait out.
drugs.dependence: Classic psychedelics have little physical dependence. They can still be misused, and some analogues are more compulsive or more toxic.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to LSD-type psychedelics rises very fast and fades over several days. That is not a dosing instruction.
drugs.withdrawal: A physical withdrawal syndrome is not typical. Low mood and anxiety after a difficult experience are.
drugs.medical_uses: A small number are in clinical research or traditional ceremonial use. That is not a reason to use them, and it is not a dose.
drugs.contraindications: Personal or family psychosis, lithium, tramadol, MAOIs, and heart disease for the physically harsh members.
drugs.testing: Blotter and powders sold as LSD are sometimes NBOMe compounds, which are more toxic. A bitter or metallic taste is a warning, not a confirmation.
drugs.harm_reduction: A sober sitter matters. Do not mix with lithium, tramadol, or MAOIs. This file has no dose and does not describe extraction.

drugs.mechanism: Solvents disrupt membranes and sensitise the heart to adrenaline. Nitrous blocks NMDA receptors. Nitrites dilate blood vessels.
drugs.onset: Seconds to minutes.

effects: dizziness
brief euphoria
flushing with nitrites
drugs.acute_risks: Sudden cardiac death from volatile solvents, frost injury and asphyxia from nitrous, and collapsed blood pressure when nitrites meet medicines like sildenafil. A nitrite sold as a room odouriser. Low blood pressure, a pounding head, eye injury, and methaemoglobinaemia. With sildenafil or similar medicines, blood pressure can collapse.
drugs.chronic_risks: Brain and nerve injury, bone-marrow suppression, liver and kidney injury, and vitamin B12 inactivation from repeated nitrous use.
drugs.overdose_signs: Collapse, irregular heart, blue skin, or not breathing. This is an emergency. Do not chase it with activity or a scare response.
drugs.dependence: Psychological dependence occurs. The dangerous pattern is repeated exposure in one session.
drugs.tolerance: Not protective. Repeating a solvent raises the chance of a fatal rhythm.
drugs.withdrawal: Cravings and low mood. The organ damage is separate.
drugs.medical_uses: Nitrous is a medical anaesthetic and a food-propellant. Volatile solvents are industrial chemicals, not medicines.
drugs.contraindications: Heart disease, pregnancy, B12 deficiency, and erection medicines for nitrites.
drugs.testing: There is no reagent test for a safer inhalant. The product is the hazard.
drugs.harm_reduction: Sudden death can happen on first use of volatile solvents. Repeated nitrous needs medical attention if fingers tingle or walking changes. This file does not describe a method.

drugs.onset: Wanted mood effects often take weeks. Side effects and interaction risks can appear with the first exposure.

effects: changed mood over weeks
changed sleep
changed appetite
drugs.acute_risks: Early agitation, and with the wrong mix, serotonin syndrome or a blood-pressure crisis. Overdose of older tricyclics can stop the heart. A tricyclic antidepressant. Heart toxicity in overdose, sedation with alcohol, and a deadly mix with MAOIs.
drugs.chronic_risks: Withdrawal symptoms if stopped suddenly, weight and metabolic change with some, and persistent sexual side effects in some people.
drugs.overdose_signs: Serotonin syndrome looks like agitation, rigidity, sweating, and a rising temperature. A tricyclic overdose looks like seizures and heart rhythm collapse. Both are emergencies.
drugs.dependence: They are not intoxicants in the opioid sense. Stopping suddenly still causes a withdrawal syndrome.
drugs.tolerance: Side effects often ease. The interaction risks do not expire.
drugs.withdrawal: Dizziness, electric-shock feelings, anxiety, and flu-like symptoms. Tapering is a medical decision.
drugs.medical_uses: Depression, anxiety, pain, and smoking cessation, depending on the drug.
drugs.contraindications: MAOIs combined with SSRIs, stimulants, tramadol, DXM, or many plant preparations. Recent heart attack for some.
drugs.testing: Not a reagent-test problem. The risk is the name on the packet plus whatever else is taken.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not combine an MAOI with an SSRI, a stimulant, tramadol, or DXM. Do not stop suddenly without the prescriber. This file has no dose.

drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.

drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.

drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. A later nitazene. Drug checking, not a vendor name, is how these are identified after the fact.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.legal_status: Control status depends on the country, the form, and sometimes the amount. This file is not legal advice.

drugs.chemistry: Psychedelic or psychedelic-like. Named for recognition and risk. Extraction and synthesis are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Many act as serotonin 5-HT2A agonists. Others in this list have different and sometimes more dangerous mechanisms.
drugs.onset: Minutes to more than an hour. A slow start is a common reason people take more and then have a much stronger effect.
drugs.duration: From under an hour to a full day or longer. Some, including DOB and related drugs, last much longer than LSD.
drugs.half_life: Often poorly studied outside a few medicines and classic psychedelics. Duration of impairment is the practical fact.
effects: altered perception
changed thinking
emotional intensity
sensory distortion
drugs.acute_risks: Panic, dangerous behaviour, and for some members of this class, seizures, overheating, heart strain, or vasoconstriction. NBOMe compounds and ibogaine are physically riskier than classic psychedelics. A synthetic tryptamine. Identity and strength of a powder are not assured by the name.
drugs.chronic_risks: Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder is uncommon but real. Frequent use is linked with lasting anxiety in some people.
drugs.overdose_signs: Seizures, collapse, chest pain, a limb that stays white and painful, or a temperature that keeps rising. Those are emergencies, not a 'bad trip' to wait out.
drugs.dependence: Classic psychedelics have little physical dependence. They can still be misused, and some analogues are more compulsive or more toxic.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to LSD-type psychedelics rises very fast and fades over several days. That is not a dosing instruction.
drugs.withdrawal: A physical withdrawal syndrome is not typical. Low mood and anxiety after a difficult experience are.
drugs.medical_uses: A small number are in clinical research or traditional ceremonial use. That is not a reason to use them, and it is not a dose.
drugs.contraindications: Personal or family psychosis, lithium, tramadol, MAOIs, and heart disease for the physically harsh members.
drugs.testing: Blotter and powders sold as LSD are sometimes NBOMe compounds, which are more toxic. A bitter or metallic taste is a warning, not a confirmation.
drugs.harm_reduction: A sober sitter matters. Do not mix with lithium, tramadol, or MAOIs. This file has no dose and does not describe extraction.

drugs.medical_status: No accepted medical product. Material in circulation is unregulated and may be mislabelled or contaminated.
drugs.chemistry: Opioid. Named here so the breathing risk can be recognised. Manufacture and extraction are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. An opioid compound from research. Breathing risk. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.chemistry: Psychedelic or psychedelic-like. Named for recognition and risk. Extraction and synthesis are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Many act as serotonin 5-HT2A agonists. Others in this list have different and sometimes more dangerous mechanisms.
drugs.onset: Minutes to more than an hour. A slow start is a common reason people take more and then have a much stronger effect.
drugs.duration: From under an hour to a full day or longer. Some, including DOB and related drugs, last much longer than LSD.
drugs.half_life: Often poorly studied outside a few medicines and classic psychedelics. Duration of impairment is the practical fact.
effects: altered perception
changed thinking
emotional intensity
sensory distortion
drugs.acute_risks: Panic, dangerous behaviour, and for some members of this class, seizures, overheating, heart strain, or vasoconstriction. NBOMe compounds and ibogaine are physically riskier than classic psychedelics. A dimethoxyamphetamine. Longer and harsher than people expect from the name. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder is uncommon but real. Frequent use is linked with lasting anxiety in some people.
drugs.overdose_signs: Seizures, collapse, chest pain, a limb that stays white and painful, or a temperature that keeps rising. Those are emergencies, not a 'bad trip' to wait out.
drugs.dependence: Classic psychedelics have little physical dependence. They can still be misused, and some analogues are more compulsive or more toxic.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to LSD-type psychedelics rises very fast and fades over several days. That is not a dosing instruction.
drugs.withdrawal: A physical withdrawal syndrome is not typical. Low mood and anxiety after a difficult experience are.
drugs.medical_uses: A small number are in clinical research or traditional ceremonial use. That is not a reason to use them, and it is not a dose.
drugs.contraindications: Personal or family psychosis, lithium, tramadol, MAOIs, and heart disease for the physically harsh members.
drugs.testing: Blotter and powders sold as LSD are sometimes NBOMe compounds, which are more toxic. A bitter or metallic taste is a warning, not a confirmation.
drugs.harm_reduction: A sober sitter matters. Do not mix with lithium, tramadol, or MAOIs. This file has no dose and does not describe extraction.

drugs.chemistry: Stimulant. Named here for the heart and temperature risk. Synthesis is outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Increases catecholamine signalling, by release, reuptake block, or both.
drugs.onset: Often minutes to an hour, depending on the substance. Fast onset does not mean the heart is safe.

effects: alertness
energy
talkativeness
reduced appetite
raised heart rate
drugs.acute_risks: Heart attack, stroke, seizure, overheating, and agitated psychosis. Risk rises with other stimulants, dehydration, and confined hot spaces. An aminopropylindole stimulant. Serotonin and heart risk with little human data. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, exhaustion, weight loss, heart injury, tooth and nasal damage for some, and persistent anxiety or psychosis.
drugs.overdose_signs: Chest pain, collapsing, extreme agitation, very high temperature, seizures, or a pounding heart. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Psychological dependence is common. Some stimulants also cause a severe crash.
drugs.tolerance: The wanted effect fades faster than the strain on the heart.
drugs.withdrawal: Exhaustion, hunger, low mood, and strong cravings. Suicidal thoughts can appear in the crash.
drugs.medical_uses: A few are licensed for attention or sleep disorders. Most stimulant material outside a pharmacy is unregulated.
drugs.contraindications: Heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, psychosis, pregnancy, and MAOI medicines.
drugs.testing: Reagents can suggest a class and still miss dangerous substitutes such as PMA, synthetic cathinones, or fentanyl in a pressed pill.
drugs.harm_reduction: Overheating and chest pain are emergencies. Do not mix with other stimulants or MAOIs. This file has no dose and no source.

drugs.chemistry: Psychedelic or psychedelic-like. Named for recognition and risk. Extraction and synthesis are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Many act as serotonin 5-HT2A agonists. Others in this list have different and sometimes more dangerous mechanisms.
drugs.onset: Minutes to more than an hour. A slow start is a common reason people take more and then have a much stronger effect.
drugs.duration: From under an hour to a full day or longer. Some, including DOB and related drugs, last much longer than LSD.
drugs.half_life: Often poorly studied outside a few medicines and classic psychedelics. Duration of impairment is the practical fact.
effects: altered perception
changed thinking
emotional intensity
sensory distortion
drugs.acute_risks: Panic, dangerous behaviour, and for some members of this class, seizures, overheating, heart strain, or vasoconstriction. NBOMe compounds and ibogaine are physically riskier than classic psychedelics. A tryptamine. Serotonin and stimulation risks are plausible and poorly studied. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Hallucinogen persisting perception disorder is uncommon but real. Frequent use is linked with lasting anxiety in some people.
drugs.overdose_signs: Seizures, collapse, chest pain, a limb that stays white and painful, or a temperature that keeps rising. Those are emergencies, not a 'bad trip' to wait out.
drugs.dependence: Classic psychedelics have little physical dependence. They can still be misused, and some analogues are more compulsive or more toxic.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to LSD-type psychedelics rises very fast and fades over several days. That is not a dosing instruction.
drugs.withdrawal: A physical withdrawal syndrome is not typical. Low mood and anxiety after a difficult experience are.
drugs.medical_uses: A small number are in clinical research or traditional ceremonial use. That is not a reason to use them, and it is not a dose.
drugs.contraindications: Personal or family psychosis, lithium, tramadol, MAOIs, and heart disease for the physically harsh members.
drugs.testing: Blotter and powders sold as LSD are sometimes NBOMe compounds, which are more toxic. A bitter or metallic taste is a warning, not a confirmation.
drugs.harm_reduction: A sober sitter matters. Do not mix with lithium, tramadol, or MAOIs. This file has no dose and does not describe extraction.

drugs.acute_risks: Immobility, accidents, vomiting while semi-conscious, and a state of being unable to move or speak. With alcohol or opioids, breathing may fail. A PCP analogue. Confusion, stimulation, and a long course. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Ketamine is linked with severe bladder damage, kidney problems, and memory injury. PCP-type drugs are linked with agitation and prolonged psychosis.
drugs.overdose_signs: Unresponsiveness, vomiting, slow breathing, seizures, or extreme overheating and agitation with PCP-type drugs. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Psychological dependence on ketamine is well described. Physical withdrawal is milder than with alcohol or opioids and still unpleasant.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises quickly with frequent ketamine use.
drugs.withdrawal: Low mood, anxiety, and cravings. Bladder symptoms do not stop just because use stops, and they need medical care.
drugs.medical_uses: Ketamine and esketamine have medical roles. Most other dissociatives do not.
drugs.contraindications: Uncontrolled high blood pressure, psychosis, active bladder disease, and other sedatives.
drugs.testing: Powders sold as ketamine may be a different dissociative of much longer duration. Reagents do not measure strength.
drugs.harm_reduction: Bladder pain and blood in urine after ketamine need a clinician, not a pause-and-retry. Do not mix with alcohol or opioids. This file has no dose.

drugs.legal_status: Control status depends on the country, the form, and sometimes the amount. This file is not legal advice.
drugs.medical_status: Licensed as a medicine in at least some countries. A prescription is not a clearance to mix it or to use it outside medical care.
drugs.chemistry: Benzodiazepine or closely related sedative. Named for the blackout and breathing risk. Synthesis is outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Positive modulator of GABA-A receptors. Raises the effect of the brain's main calming signal.
drugs.onset: Often within an hour for swallowed forms. Faster routes are not described here and are not safer.
drugs.duration: From a few hours to several days, depending on the drug and its active metabolites.
drugs.half_life: Some are short. Others, and their metabolites, last for days and stack if repeated.
effects: reduced anxiety
sleepiness
muscle relaxation
memory gaps
drugs.acute_risks: Amnesia, injury, and sexual vulnerability during blackouts. With alcohol or opioids, breathing can stop. A benzodiazepine used in a few countries. Dependence and sedative mixes follow the class.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, worsened anxiety between uses, falls in older people, and a hard withdrawal.
drugs.overdose_signs: Extreme sedation. If an opioid or alcohol is also involved: slow breathing and unresponsiveness. That is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Dependence can develop within weeks of regular use.
drugs.tolerance: The calming effect fades. The withdrawal risk does not.
drugs.withdrawal: Rebound anxiety, insomnia, perceptual changes, and seizures. Stopping suddenly after regular use can be a medical emergency.
drugs.medical_uses: Licensed for short-term anxiety, seizures, muscle spasm, or anaesthesia. Many circulating tablets are not the medicine named on them.
drugs.contraindications: Opioids, alcohol, other sedatives, sleep apnoea, and pregnancy.
drugs.testing: Pressed tablets are frequently a different benzodiazepine, or several. Reagents cannot tell strength.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not mix with opioids or alcohol. Do not stop regular use suddenly. This file has no dose.

drugs.chemistry: Sedative. Named here for the unconsciousness and breathing risk. Preparation is outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Calms central nervous system signalling, often through GABA or related pathways.
drugs.onset: Minutes to a couple of hours. GHB-type sedatives can go from awake to unconscious very quickly.
drugs.duration: Several hours is common. Impairment can outlast the feeling of being affected.
drugs.half_life: From short, as with GHB, to days, as with some barbiturates.
effects: relaxation
sleepiness
reduced anxiety
poor coordination
drugs.acute_risks: Unconsciousness, choking on vomit, stopped breathing, and accidents. Another sedative, opioid, or benzodiazepine makes this much more dangerous. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. This file has no dose. A hospital sedative related to medetomidine. Heart rate and blood pressure fall. It does not replace breathing support, and it is not reversed by naloxone.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, memory injury, mood change, and for alcohol, liver, heart, and cancer risk.
drugs.overdose_signs: Cannot be woken, slow or stopped breathing, blue lips, vomiting while semi-conscious. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence occurs with repeated heavy use of alcohol, barbiturates, GHB, and related sedatives.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to the feeling rises faster than tolerance to stopped breathing.
drugs.withdrawal: Alcohol, barbiturate, and GHB withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium and can be fatal. Stopping suddenly after heavy use needs medical care.
drugs.medical_uses: Some are anaesthetics, antiseizure medicines, or alcohol treatments. Others have no safe nonmedical use.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, lung disease, a history of withdrawal seizures, and pregnancy.
drugs.testing: Strength of non-pharmaceutical GHB-type liquids is unknowable by looking. Reagents do not make a sedative safe.
drugs.harm_reduction: Sedative withdrawal can kill. Do not stop heavy use suddenly without medical help. Do not mix sedatives. This file has no dose.

drugs.acute_risks: Sudden cardiac death from volatile solvents, frost injury and asphyxia from nitrous, and collapsed blood pressure when nitrites meet medicines like sildenafil. A solvent in paints. Sudden heart rhythm death and brain injury with repeated inhalation. This file has no method.

drugs.contraindications: Heart disease, pregnancy, B12 deficiency, and erection medicines for nitrites.

sleepiness

drugs.acute_risks: Unconsciousness, choking on vomit, stopped breathing, and accidents. Another sedative, opioid, or benzodiazepine makes this much more dangerous. drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, memory injury, mood change, and for alcohol, liver, heart, and cancer risk.
drugs.overdose_signs: Cannot be woken, slow or stopped breathing, blue lips, vomiting while semi-conscious. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence occurs with repeated heavy use of alcohol, barbiturates, GHB, and related sedatives.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to the feeling rises faster than tolerance to stopped breathing.
drugs.withdrawal: Alcohol, barbiturate, and GHB withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium and can be fatal. Stopping suddenly after heavy use needs medical care.
drugs.medical_uses: Some are anaesthetics, antiseizure medicines, or alcohol treatments. Others have no safe nonmedical use.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, lung disease, a history of withdrawal seizures, and pregnancy.
drugs.testing: Strength of non-pharmaceutical GHB-type liquids is unknowable by looking. Reagents do not make a sedative safe.
drugs.harm_reduction: Sedative withdrawal can kill. Do not stop heavy use suddenly without medical help. Do not mix sedatives. This file has no dose.

drugs.chronic_risks: Brain and nerve injury, bone-marrow suppression, liver and kidney injury, and vitamin B12 inactivation from repeated nitrous use.
drugs.overdose_signs: Collapse, irregular heart, blue skin, or not breathing. This is an emergency. Do not chase it with activity or a scare response.

drugs.contraindications: Heart disease, pregnancy, B12 deficiency, and erection medicines for nitrites.

drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.

drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.

drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

brief euphoria

drugs.acute_risks: Sudden cardiac death from volatile solvents, frost injury and asphyxia from nitrous, and collapsed blood pressure when nitrites meet medicines like sildenafil. drugs.chronic_risks: Brain and nerve injury, bone-marrow suppression, liver and kidney injury, and vitamin B12 inactivation from repeated nitrous use.
drugs.overdose_signs: Collapse, irregular heart, blue skin, or not breathing. This is an emergency. Do not chase it with activity or a scare response.
drugs.dependence: Psychological dependence occurs. The dangerous pattern is repeated exposure in one session.
drugs.tolerance: Not protective. Repeating a solvent raises the chance of a fatal rhythm.
drugs.withdrawal: Cravings and low mood. The organ damage is separate.
drugs.medical_uses: Nitrous is a medical anaesthetic and a food-propellant. Volatile solvents are industrial chemicals, not medicines.
drugs.contraindications: Heart disease, pregnancy, B12 deficiency, and erection medicines for nitrites.
drugs.testing: There is no reagent test for a safer inhalant. The product is the hazard.
drugs.harm_reduction: Sudden death can happen on first use of volatile solvents. Repeated nitrous needs medical attention if fingers tingle or walking changes. This file does not describe a method.

drugs.chemistry: Sedative. Named here for the unconsciousness and breathing risk. Preparation is outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Calms central nervous system signalling, often through GABA or related pathways.
drugs.onset: Minutes to a couple of hours. GHB-type sedatives can go from awake to unconscious very quickly.
drugs.duration: Several hours is common. Impairment can outlast the feeling of being affected.
drugs.half_life: From short, as with GHB, to days, as with some barbiturates.
effects: relaxation
sleepiness
reduced anxiety
poor coordination
drugs.acute_risks: Unconsciousness, choking on vomit, stopped breathing, and accidents. Another sedative, opioid, or benzodiazepine makes this much more dangerous. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. A barbiturate sedative. Overdose stops breathing. Withdrawal can cause seizures and can kill. With an opioid the breathing risk multiplies. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, memory injury, mood change, and for alcohol, liver, heart, and cancer risk.
drugs.overdose_signs: Cannot be woken, slow or stopped breathing, blue lips, vomiting while semi-conscious. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence occurs with repeated heavy use of alcohol, barbiturates, GHB, and related sedatives.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to the feeling rises faster than tolerance to stopped breathing.
drugs.withdrawal: Alcohol, barbiturate, and GHB withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium and can be fatal. Stopping suddenly after heavy use needs medical care.
drugs.medical_uses: Some are anaesthetics, antiseizure medicines, or alcohol treatments. Others have no safe nonmedical use.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, lung disease, a history of withdrawal seizures, and pregnancy.
drugs.testing: Strength of non-pharmaceutical GHB-type liquids is unknowable by looking. Reagents do not make a sedative safe.
drugs.harm_reduction: Sedative withdrawal can kill. Do not stop heavy use suddenly without medical help. Do not mix sedatives. This file has no dose.

drugs.chemistry: Sedative. Named here for the unconsciousness and breathing risk. Preparation is outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Calms central nervous system signalling, often through GABA or related pathways.
drugs.onset: Minutes to a couple of hours. GHB-type sedatives can go from awake to unconscious very quickly.
drugs.duration: Several hours is common. Impairment can outlast the feeling of being affected.
drugs.half_life: From short, as with GHB, to days, as with some barbiturates.
effects: relaxation
sleepiness
reduced anxiety
poor coordination
drugs.acute_risks: Unconsciousness, choking on vomit, stopped breathing, and accidents. Another sedative, opioid, or benzodiazepine makes this much more dangerous. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. A muscle relaxant with sedative effects. With an opioid or alcohol someone can stop protecting the airway. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, memory injury, mood change, and for alcohol, liver, heart, and cancer risk.
drugs.overdose_signs: Cannot be woken, slow or stopped breathing, blue lips, vomiting while semi-conscious. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence occurs with repeated heavy use of alcohol, barbiturates, GHB, and related sedatives.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to the feeling rises faster than tolerance to stopped breathing.
drugs.withdrawal: Alcohol, barbiturate, and GHB withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium and can be fatal. Stopping suddenly after heavy use needs medical care.
drugs.medical_uses: Some are anaesthetics, antiseizure medicines, or alcohol treatments. Others have no safe nonmedical use.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, lung disease, a history of withdrawal seizures, and pregnancy.
drugs.testing: Strength of non-pharmaceutical GHB-type liquids is unknowable by looking. Reagents do not make a sedative safe.
drugs.harm_reduction: Sedative withdrawal can kill. Do not stop heavy use suddenly without medical help. Do not mix sedatives. This file has no dose.

poor coordination

drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, memory injury, mood change, and for alcohol, liver, heart, and cancer risk.

drugs.dependence: Physical dependence occurs with repeated heavy use of alcohol, barbiturates, GHB, and related sedatives.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to the feeling rises faster than tolerance to stopped breathing.

drugs.medical_uses: Some are anaesthetics, antiseizure medicines, or alcohol treatments. Others have no safe nonmedical use.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, lung disease, a history of withdrawal seizures, and pregnancy.
drugs.testing: Strength of non-pharmaceutical GHB-type liquids is unknowable by looking. Reagents do not make a sedative safe.
drugs.harm_reduction: Sedative withdrawal can kill. Do not stop heavy use suddenly without medical help. Do not mix sedatives. This file has no dose.

An antiviral used for HIV or hepatitis. Stopping and restarting can let the virus escape. Some of these block or induce liver enzymes and change the levels of many other drugs. This file is not a regimen. This file has no dose. This is not a dose, a source, or a reason to use it.

drugs.mechanism: Calms central nervous system signalling, often through GABA or related pathways.
drugs.onset: Minutes to a couple of hours. GHB-type sedatives can go from awake to unconscious very quickly.
drugs.duration: Several hours is common. Impairment can outlast the feeling of being affected.
drugs.half_life: From short, as with GHB, to days, as with some barbiturates.
effects: relaxation
sleepiness
reduced anxiety
poor coordination
drugs.acute_risks: Unconsciousness, choking on vomit, stopped breathing, and accidents. Another sedative, opioid, or benzodiazepine makes this much more dangerous. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. A muscle relaxant with sedative effects. With an opioid or alcohol someone can stop protecting the airway. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, memory injury, mood change, and for alcohol, liver, heart, and cancer risk.
drugs.overdose_signs: Cannot be woken, slow or stopped breathing, blue lips, vomiting while semi-conscious. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence occurs with repeated heavy use of alcohol, barbiturates, GHB, and related sedatives.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to the feeling rises faster than tolerance to stopped breathing.
drugs.withdrawal: Alcohol, barbiturate, and GHB withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium and can be fatal. Stopping suddenly after heavy use needs medical care.
drugs.medical_uses: Some are anaesthetics, antiseizure medicines, or alcohol treatments. Others have no safe nonmedical use.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, lung disease, a history of withdrawal seizures, and pregnancy.
drugs.testing: Strength of non-pharmaceutical GHB-type liquids is unknowable by looking. Reagents do not make a sedative safe.
drugs.harm_reduction: Sedative withdrawal can kill. Do not stop heavy use suddenly without medical help. Do not mix sedatives. This file has no dose.

drugs.acute_risks: Early agitation, and with the wrong mix, serotonin syndrome or a blood-pressure crisis. Overdose of older tricyclics can stop the heart. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. A tricyclic antidepressant. Overdose can seize and stop the heart. With an MAOI the mix is contraindicated. It also sedates and can drop blood pressure. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Withdrawal symptoms if stopped suddenly, weight and metabolic change with some, and persistent sexual side effects in some people.
drugs.overdose_signs: Serotonin syndrome looks like agitation, rigidity, sweating, and a rising temperature. A tricyclic overdose looks like seizures and heart rhythm collapse. Both are emergencies.

drugs.tolerance: Side effects often ease. The interaction risks do not expire.
drugs.withdrawal: Dizziness, electric-shock feelings, anxiety, and flu-like symptoms. Tapering is a medical decision.
drugs.medical_uses: Depression, anxiety, pain, and smoking cessation, depending on the drug.
drugs.contraindications: MAOIs combined with SSRIs, stimulants, tramadol, DXM, or many plant preparations. Recent heart attack for some.
drugs.testing: Not a reagent-test problem. The risk is the name on the packet plus whatever else is taken.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not combine an MAOI with an SSRI, a stimulant, tramadol, or DXM. Do not stop suddenly without the prescriber. This file has no dose.

With an MAOI the mix can be a hypertensive crisis. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, exhaustion, weight loss, heart injury, tooth and nasal damage for some, and persistent anxiety or psychosis.
drugs.overdose_signs: Chest pain, collapsing, extreme agitation, very high temperature, seizures, or a pounding heart. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Psychological dependence is common. Some stimulants also cause a severe crash.
drugs.tolerance: The wanted effect fades faster than the strain on the heart.
drugs.withdrawal: Exhaustion, hunger, low mood, and strong cravings. Suicidal thoughts can appear in the crash.
drugs.medical_uses: A few are licensed for attention or sleep disorders. Most stimulant material outside a pharmacy is unregulated.
drugs.contraindications: Heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, psychosis, pregnancy, and MAOI medicines.
drugs.testing: Reagents can suggest a class and still miss dangerous substitutes such as PMA, synthetic cathinones, or fentanyl in a pressed pill.
drugs.harm_reduction: Overheating and chest pain are emergencies. Do not mix with other stimulants or MAOIs. This file has no dose and no source.

drugs.chemistry: Sedative. Named here for the unconsciousness and breathing risk. Preparation is outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Calms central nervous system signalling, often through GABA or related pathways.
drugs.onset: Minutes to a couple of hours. GHB-type sedatives can go from awake to unconscious very quickly.
drugs.duration: Several hours is common. Impairment can outlast the feeling of being affected.
drugs.half_life: From short, as with GHB, to days, as with some barbiturates.
effects: relaxation
sleepiness
reduced anxiety
poor coordination
drugs.acute_risks: Unconsciousness, choking on vomit, stopped breathing, and accidents. Another sedative, opioid, or benzodiazepine makes this much more dangerous. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. A muscle relaxant with sedative effects. With an opioid or alcohol someone can stop protecting the airway. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, memory injury, mood change, and for alcohol, liver, heart, and cancer risk.
drugs.overdose_signs: Cannot be woken, slow or stopped breathing, blue lips, vomiting while semi-conscious. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence occurs with repeated heavy use of alcohol, barbiturates, GHB, and related sedatives.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance to the feeling rises faster than tolerance to stopped breathing.
drugs.withdrawal: Alcohol, barbiturate, and GHB withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium and can be fatal. Stopping suddenly after heavy use needs medical care.
drugs.medical_uses: Some are anaesthetics, antiseizure medicines, or alcohol treatments. Others have no safe nonmedical use.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, lung disease, a history of withdrawal seizures, and pregnancy.
drugs.testing: Strength of non-pharmaceutical GHB-type liquids is unknowable by looking. Reagents do not make a sedative safe.
drugs.harm_reduction: Sedative withdrawal can kill. Do not stop heavy use suddenly without medical help. Do not mix sedatives. This file has no dose.

With an SSRI, a stimulant, tramadol, DXM, or many plant preparations it can cause serotonin syndrome or a blood-pressure crisis. A washout is a medical decision. This file has no taper plan. This file has no dose. This is not a dose, a source, or a reason to use it.

It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. An MAO inhibitor. drugs.chronic_risks: Withdrawal symptoms if stopped suddenly, weight and metabolic change with some, and persistent sexual side effects in some people.
drugs.overdose_signs: Serotonin syndrome looks like agitation, rigidity, sweating, and a rising temperature. A tricyclic overdose looks like seizures and heart rhythm collapse. Both are emergencies.
drugs.dependence: They are not intoxicants in the opioid sense. Stopping suddenly still causes a withdrawal syndrome.
drugs.tolerance: Side effects often ease. The interaction risks do not expire.
drugs.withdrawal: Dizziness, electric-shock feelings, anxiety, and flu-like symptoms. Tapering is a medical decision.
drugs.medical_uses: Depression, anxiety, pain, and smoking cessation, depending on the drug.
drugs.contraindications: MAOIs combined with SSRIs, stimulants, tramadol, DXM, or many plant preparations. Recent heart attack for some.
drugs.testing: Not a reagent-test problem. The risk is the name on the packet plus whatever else is taken.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not combine an MAOI with an SSRI, a stimulant, tramadol, or DXM. Do not stop suddenly without the prescriber. This file has no dose.

drugs.medical_status: Licensed as a medicine in at least some countries. A prescription is not a clearance to mix it or to use it outside medical care.
drugs.chemistry: Stimulant. Named here for the heart and temperature risk. Synthesis is outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Increases catecholamine signalling, by release, reuptake block, or both.
drugs.onset: Often minutes to an hour, depending on the substance. Fast onset does not mean the heart is safe.
drugs.duration: Hours, sometimes with a long crash afterwards. Some substituted cathinones last longer than people expect.
drugs.half_life: Highly variable. Residual stimulation and a low mood can outlast the wanted effect.
effects: alertness
energy
talkativeness
reduced appetite
raised heart rate
drugs.acute_risks: Heart attack, stroke, seizure, overheating, and agitated psychosis. Risk rises with other stimulants, dehydration, and confined hot spaces. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. A stimulant or stimulant-class ADHD medicine. The heart rate and blood pressure rise. With an MAOI the mix can be a hypertensive crisis. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, exhaustion, weight loss, heart injury, tooth and nasal damage for some, and persistent anxiety or psychosis.
drugs.overdose_signs: Chest pain, collapsing, extreme agitation, very high temperature, seizures, or a pounding heart. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Psychological dependence is common. Some stimulants also cause a severe crash.
drugs.tolerance: The wanted effect fades faster than the strain on the heart.
drugs.withdrawal: Exhaustion, hunger, low mood, and strong cravings. Suicidal thoughts can appear in the crash.
drugs.medical_uses: A few are licensed for attention or sleep disorders. Most stimulant material outside a pharmacy is unregulated.
drugs.contraindications: Heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, psychosis, pregnancy, and MAOI medicines.
drugs.testing: Reagents can suggest a class and still miss dangerous substitutes such as PMA, synthetic cathinones, or fentanyl in a pressed pill.
drugs.harm_reduction: Overheating and chest pain are emergencies. Do not mix with other stimulants or MAOIs. This file has no dose and no source.

drugs.acute_risks: Unconsciousness, choking on vomit, stopped breathing, and accidents. Another sedative, opioid, or benzodiazepine makes this much more dangerous. drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, lung disease, a history of withdrawal seizures, and pregnancy.

drugs.harm_reduction: Sedative withdrawal can kill. Do not stop heavy use suddenly without medical help. Do not mix sedatives. This file has no dose.

drugs.chemistry: Opioid. Named here so the breathing risk can be recognised. Manufacture and extraction are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. An opioid. Breathing slows, and a benzodiazepine, alcohol, or another sedative can make that fatal. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

effects: alertness
energy
talkativeness
reduced appetite
raised heart rate
drugs.acute_risks: Heart attack, stroke, seizure, overheating, and agitated psychosis. Risk rises with other stimulants, dehydration, and confined hot spaces. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. A stimulant or stimulant-class ADHD medicine. The heart rate and blood pressure rise. With an MAOI the mix can be a hypertensive crisis. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Dependence, exhaustion, weight loss, heart injury, tooth and nasal damage for some, and persistent anxiety or psychosis.
drugs.overdose_signs: Chest pain, collapsing, extreme agitation, very high temperature, seizures, or a pounding heart. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Psychological dependence is common. Some stimulants also cause a severe crash.
drugs.tolerance: The wanted effect fades faster than the strain on the heart.
drugs.withdrawal: Exhaustion, hunger, low mood, and strong cravings. Suicidal thoughts can appear in the crash.
drugs.medical_uses: A few are licensed for attention or sleep disorders. Most stimulant material outside a pharmacy is unregulated.
drugs.contraindications: Heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, psychosis, pregnancy, and MAOI medicines.
drugs.testing: Reagents can suggest a class and still miss dangerous substitutes such as PMA, synthetic cathinones, or fentanyl in a pressed pill.
drugs.harm_reduction: Overheating and chest pain are emergencies. Do not mix with other stimulants or MAOIs. This file has no dose and no source.

drugs.chemistry: Opioid. Named here so the breathing risk can be recognised. Manufacture and extraction are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. An opioid that stays in the gut at ordinary use. Very high exposure has stopped the heart. This file does not describe taking more. Sedatives still add risk. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.onset: Minutes when absorbed quickly, longer otherwise. This file does not describe routes.
drugs.duration: About an hour for some, and many hours for PCP-type drugs.
drugs.half_life: Ketamine is relatively short. PCP-type drugs and some research dissociatives last much longer.
effects: detachment
analgesia
distorted body sense
anaesthesia at high exposure
drugs.acute_risks: Immobility, accidents, vomiting while semi-conscious, and a state of being unable to move or speak. With alcohol or opioids, breathing may fail. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. A cough medicine and a dissociative. With an MAOI it can cause severe serotonin syndrome. With an SSRI the serotonin risk is real. Combination bottles often hide other sedatives or paracetamol. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Ketamine is linked with severe bladder damage, kidney problems, and memory injury. PCP-type drugs are linked with agitation and prolonged psychosis.
drugs.overdose_signs: Unresponsiveness, vomiting, slow breathing, seizures, or extreme overheating and agitation with PCP-type drugs. This is an emergency.
drugs.dependence: Psychological dependence on ketamine is well described. Physical withdrawal is milder than with alcohol or opioids and still unpleasant.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises quickly with frequent ketamine use.
drugs.withdrawal: Low mood, anxiety, and cravings. Bladder symptoms do not stop just because use stops, and they need medical care.
drugs.medical_uses: Ketamine and esketamine have medical roles. Most other dissociatives do not.
drugs.contraindications: Uncontrolled high blood pressure, psychosis, active bladder disease, and other sedatives.
drugs.testing: Powders sold as ketamine may be a different dissociative of much longer duration. Reagents do not measure strength.
drugs.harm_reduction: Bladder pain and blood in urine after ketamine need a clinician, not a pause-and-retry. Do not mix with alcohol or opioids. This file has no dose.

drugs.chemistry: Opioid. Named here so the breathing risk can be recognised. Manufacture and extraction are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. An opioid. Breathing slows, and a benzodiazepine, alcohol, or another sedative can make that fatal. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. An opioid. Breathing slows, and a benzodiazepine, alcohol, or another sedative can make that fatal. The anti-inflammatory half adds a bleeding risk. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. An opioid. Breathing slows, and a benzodiazepine, alcohol, or another sedative can make that fatal. An antagonist in the same product does not make a mix with alcohol or a benzodiazepine safe. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.

effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.

drugs.chemistry: Opioid. Named here so the breathing risk can be recognised. Manufacture and extraction are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. An opioid that stays in the gut at ordinary use. Very high exposure has stopped the heart. This file does not describe taking more. Sedatives still add risk. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

Sodium and potassium can fall. Lithium can rise. With an NSAID and an ACE inhibitor the kidneys can fail. Loop diuretics also add hearing injury with some antibiotics. This file has no dose. This is not a dose, a source, or a reason to use it.

sleepiness
reduced anxiety
poor coordination

drugs.chemistry: Opioid. Named here so the breathing risk can be recognised. Manufacture and extraction are outside this archive.
drugs.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor activity. Breathing slows as the effect deepens.
drugs.onset: Depends on the substance and the route. Some act in minutes. Others take much longer, which is when people get into trouble by taking more.
drugs.duration: Often several hours. Some synthetic opioids last much longer than naloxone.
drugs.half_life: Ranges from short to very long. A person can look awake and still stop breathing later.
effects: pain relief
sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. An opioid. Breathing slows, and a benzodiazepine, alcohol, or another sedative can make that fatal. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.

drugs.chronic_risks: Withdrawal symptoms if stopped suddenly, weight and metabolic change with some, and persistent sexual side effects in some people.

drugs.tolerance: Side effects often ease. The interaction risks do not expire.
drugs.withdrawal: Dizziness, electric-shock feelings, anxiety, and flu-like symptoms. Tapering is a medical decision.
drugs.medical_uses: Depression, anxiety, pain, and smoking cessation, depending on the drug.
drugs.contraindications: MAOIs combined with SSRIs, stimulants, tramadol, DXM, or many plant preparations. Recent heart attack for some.
drugs.testing: Not a reagent-test problem. The risk is the name on the packet plus whatever else is taken.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not combine an MAOI with an SSRI, a stimulant, tramadol, or DXM. Do not stop suddenly without the prescriber. This file has no dose.

sedation
euphoria
slowed breathing
drugs.acute_risks: The acute danger is slowed or stopped breathing. Alcohol, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives multiply that risk. Non-pharmaceutical material may contain fentanyl, nitazenes, or xylazine. It is in this index because it changes the risk of other substances. This is not a prescribing guide. An opioid. Breathing slows, and a benzodiazepine, alcohol, or another sedative can make that fatal. This file has no dose.
drugs.chronic_risks: Tolerance, dependence, constipation, low sex hormones, and fatal overdose are the main long-term harms.
drugs.overdose_signs: Slow or stopped breathing, blue or grey lips, gurgling, unresponsiveness, pinpoint pupils. This is an emergency. Naloxone can reverse the opioid and may need repeating.
drugs.dependence: Physical dependence is common with repeated use.
drugs.tolerance: Tolerance rises with repeated use, then falls after a break. A familiar amount can become fatal after a pause.
drugs.withdrawal: Withdrawal feels like a severe flu with cramps, sweating, and distress. It is rarely fatal by itself and it raises the chance of returning to use.
drugs.medical_uses: Some opioids are pain or addiction medicines. Many have no accepted role outside a hospital, or none at all.
drugs.contraindications: Other sedatives, sleep apnoea, severe lung disease, and unknown-strength material.
drugs.testing: Fentanyl strips and reagent colours miss analogues and do not measure strength. A negative test is not proof of safety.
drugs.harm_reduction: Do not use alone. Keep naloxone nearby and make sure another person knows how to use it. A blank mix result is not a green light. This file has no dose.
